CausalChain: Radiotherapy → Tumor cell death and neoantigen release → Activation of systemic and tumor immune responses (STIE and TIME) → Induction of tumor-associated ter cells → Secretion of Artemin → Binding of Artemin to GFRα3 on tumor and stromal cells → Suppression of CD8+ T cell activation and infiltration → Reduced efficacy of PD-1 inhibitor therapy → Hypothesized benefit of Artemin inhibition to restore immune function and boost therapeutic response
Hypothesis: In solid tumors such as NSCLC, inhibition of Artemin signaling can disrupt the tumor-induced immunosuppressive loop in the TIME post-radiotherapy, thereby enhancing CD8+ T cell-mediated responses and improving the efficacy of PD-1 checkpoint blockade immunotherapy.
Abstract: Recent advances in immunotherapy have highlighted the crucial role of both the systemic tumor immune environment (STIE) and the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) in determining treatment efficacy. Radiotherapy, by inducing tumor cell death and subsequent neoantigen release, triggers an immune‐activating cascade; however, emerging evidence indicates that tumor‐induced cells, such as erythroblast‐like Ter cells, can secrete immunosuppressive factors including Artemin. Artemin, via its receptor GFRα3, can alter the local immune landscape by inhibiting effector T cell activation and infiltration. We propose a novel mechanism whereby Artemin acts as a key mediator of radio‐immunotherapy resistance by sustaining an immunosuppressive TIME that diminishes the response to PD‐1 blockade. In this context, targeting Artemin signaling may serve as an effective strategy to enhance the therapeutic synergy between radiotherapy and checkpoint inhibition in solid tumors such as non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
